body.text: A time and materials (T&M) contract pays a contractor for actual labor hours at predetermined rates plus direct material costs. For U.S. R&D tax credit purposes under IRC Section 41, a Straight T&M contract places the financial risk on the paying client, allowing that client, not the contractor, to claim 65 percent of qualifying payments as contract research expenses.
Executive Summary and Contractual Mechanics in Outsourced Research

Time and Materials (T&M) contracts are commercial procurement arrangements in which a service provider is compensated according to actual labor hours expended at predetermined hourly or daily billing rates, combined with the direct reimbursement of specific supply and material costs incurred during project execution. In research and development (R&D) environments, this contractual architecture is essential because it allows immediate project commencement and provides operational flexibility when the precise technical scope, methodology, or final design is technologically uncertain or entirely unknown at the outset. By enabling the client to pay for labor and materials as they are incurred, the T&M model removes the necessity for the exhaustive upfront bidding and scoping characteristic of fixed-price (lump-sum) contracts, thereby aligning its commercial flexibility with the experimental nature required under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41).

From a legal and economic perspective, the defining consequence of a Straight T&M contract is the asymmetric allocation of execution and financial risk between the contracting parties. Because the performing contractor is guaranteed reimbursement for time expended and materials consumed regardless of whether the project achieves technical viability, the contractor assumes negligible financial risk of research failure and secures predictable margins tied to effort rather than outcome. Conversely, the client (the paying taxpayer) deliberately shoulders the full economic exposure that the incurred expenditures may yield no usable commercial or technical deliverable.

Under United States federal tax law, this economic risk transfer governs eligibility for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities (the R&D tax credit) under IRC Section 41. Specifically, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) establishes the "funded research" exclusion, which mandates that qualified research cannot be funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. When R&D is outsourced under a Straight T&M contract, the guaranteed payment stream renders the research "funded" from the perspective of the performing contractor under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d) (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)), disqualifying the contractor from claiming the credit. Simultaneously, provided the written agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, stipulates that payment is non-contingent on the successful outcome of the research, and preserves the client's right to the research results as performed "on behalf of" the client under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), the T&M framework positions the client to claim 65 percent of the qualifying payments as Contract Research Expenses (CREs) under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A). This structural dichotomy enforces the statutory single-claimant mandate, preventing both the client and the contractor from claiming the R&D tax credit for the same underlying research activity and ensuring that the tax benefit accrues solely to the party that satisfies the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) financial risk and rights tests.
Statutory and Regulatory Framework for Contract Research Expenses
IRC Section 41 and the Four-Part Qualification Test

To qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41(d)(1) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(a), outsourced activities governed by a T&M agreement must first satisfy the statutory four-part test defining "qualified research." First, the research must serve a permitted (qualified) purpose under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and Section 41(d)(3)(A) (as implemented by 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)), meaning the activity is intended to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component—defined under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer—rather than relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Second, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(4), the investigative activity must be technological in nature, meaning the process of experimentation used to discover information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) (incorporating the Section 174 standard of 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), the project must confront technological uncertainty at its outset, meaning that information available to the taxpayer is insufficient to establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that component. Fourth, under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and (a)(6), substantially all of the developmental activities (defined by regulation as 80 percent or more of the research activities measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis for that business component) must constitute elements of a process of experimentation, involving an evaluative process of identifying alternatives and conducting modeling, simulation, or systematic trial-and-error hypothesis testing designed to resolve the underlying technical uncertainties. Where an overall business component does not meet these requirements, the "shrinking-back rule" of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) requires applying the four-part test to the most significant subset of elements of the product or process until a qualifying subcomponent is identified.

From an analytical standpoint, a taxpayer's commercial decision to execute a Straight T&M agreement for external development provides corroborating evidence that the underlying activity inherently satisfies the statutory requirement of technological uncertainty under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i). When engineering parameters are well-established and design pathways are predictable, commercial counterparties routinely lock in fixed-price terms. The fact that the scope and cost cannot be predetermined through a fixed-price model indicates that the capability, method, or appropriate design of the component remains unresolved at project inception, necessitating the flexible, effort-based payment structure of a T&M agreement. Consequently, the commercial necessity of a T&M structure directly reinforces the statutory validity of the taxpayer's claim that the outsourced activities are genuinely experimental and lack a predefined scope.
Qualified Research Expenses and Geographic Boundaries

Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) form the quantitative basis for computing the R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41(b)(1), offering a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability for costs paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business that satisfy specific IRS criteria. Under IRC Section 41(b)(1)–(3) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2, statutory QREs encompass two overarching categories—in-house research expenses and Contract Research Expenses (CREs)—which break down into primary expenditure classifications: eligible domestic employee wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and § 41(b)(2)(D), covering direct conduct, direct first-line supervision, or direct support of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(B)), the cost of qualified supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C)), certain computer rental or lease costs used in qualified research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)), and Contract Research Expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)). Qualified supplies must consist of tangible property consumed directly in the conduct of qualified research that is neither land (or improvements to land) nor property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation, such as chemical reagents or raw material components utilized for the fabrication and testing of experimental prototypes.

When utilizing T&M contracts, corporate taxpayers must exercise strict expense segregation regarding pass-through billing from the contractor under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(1). Although a T&M contractor bills for all incurred labor hours and material outlays under the commercial terms of the agreement, only the portion of the cost directly attributable to qualified research physically performed within the United States (or Puerto Rico and U.S. possessions, per the foreign research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)) is eligible for inclusion as a QRE. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(b), (c)(3), and (e)(1), pass-through expenditures for supplies or labor that are only indirectly related to R&D—such as general and administrative (G&A) overhead, accounting, payroll preparation, travel, foreign-performed labor, or non-research-related project management costs—do not constitute qualified services and must be rigorously identified and excluded from the claimed QRE pool.
The 65 Percent Statutory Inclusion Rule Under IRC Section 41(b)(3)

Contract Research Expenses represent a distinct category of QREs governed by IRC Section 41(b)(3) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e), which stipulate that the term CRE means 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on a trade or business to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for the performance on behalf of the taxpayer of qualified research (or services which, if performed by an employee of the taxpayer, would constitute qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)). (Higher statutory inclusion rates of 75 percent under IRC § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100 percent under IRC § 41(b)(3)(D) apply solely to payments made to qualified nonprofit scientific research consortia or for qualified energy research performed by eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories, leaving standard commercial T&M arrangements strictly subject to the 65 percent cap of § 41(b)(3)(A)).

In corporate tax practice, this 65 percent inclusion rule frequently leads to a critical compliance misunderstanding in which taxpayers assume the complementary 35 percent statutory reduction is intended to absorb non-qualified contractor expenses. In legal and regulatory application under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(1), where a contract calls for both qualified research services and non-qualifying services, "only 65 percent of the portion of the amount paid or incurred that is attributable to the [qualified] services... is a contract research expense." The 35 percent statutory haircut represents an automatic legislative reduction intended to strip out the contractor's assumed profit margin and indirect overhead embedded within commercial billing rates, and it is applied only after the taxpayer has identified and subtracted all non-qualifying costs—such as G&A, travel, installation, training, or purely administrative effort—from the total amount billed by the contractor. The taxpayer must therefore substantiate 100 percent of the underlying invoice base as directly attributable to qualified domestic research activities before multiplying the remaining pure research expenditure by 65 percent:

This two-stage filtration imposes an exceptionally high administrative and documentation burden on the taxpayer claiming the CRE, as summarized invoices lacking task-level granularity invalidate the 100 percent qualifying base required prior to applying the 0.65 statutory multiplier.
Contractual Risk Allocation and the Funded Research Exclusion
The Dual Mandate of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d)

The foundational legal barrier to claiming the R&D tax credit for outsourced work is the funded research exclusion codified in IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H), which states that qualified research excludes any research to the extent it is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. This statutory exclusion is interpreted and operationalized through Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d) (which governs the performing contractor's eligibility and was recently upheld against a post-Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024) regulatory validity challenge by the U.S. Tax Court in Smith v. Commissioner in 2026) in tandem with Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3) (which governs the paying client's CRE eligibility), establishing two mandatory legal standards: the financial risk test and the substantial rights test.

Under the first prong, the financial risk test, a taxpayer claiming the R&D credit—whether directly as a performer under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) or indirectly as a CRE claimant under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)—must bear the economic risk of the research work performed. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), amounts payable under any agreement that are "contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding"; conversely, research is deemed "funded" and therefore ineligible for the credit in the hands of the performer if the taxpayer performing the work receives payment that is not contingent upon the technical success of the research. Symmetrically, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) provides that a client's payment qualifies as a CRE only if the agreement "requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful," explicitly stating that if payment is contingent on the success of the research, the payment is for the product or result rather than the performance of research and is excluded from CREs.

This regulatory architecture creates a sharp dichotomy regarding T&M contracts. For the client claiming the CRE, Straight T&M contracts serve as the most favorable vehicle to satisfy the financial risk test of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) because the client is unconditionally obligated to pay the contractor for all time expended and materials consumed even if the research yields no usable or successful result, demonstrating that the client bears the financial risk of failure. Conversely, cost-plus, cost-reimbursable, hourly, and Straight T&M contracts are specifically categorized as procurement structures that generally preclude the performing contractor from claiming the credit under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Because the contractor's compensation is guaranteed by effort expended rather than technical success, the contractor is insulated from economic loss if the R&D effort fails, which is the exact reason a Straight T&M contract disqualifies the contractor while qualifying the client.

Under the second prong, the substantial rights test, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) dictate that research is deemed fully funded if the taxpayer performing the research retains "no substantial rights" in the resulting intellectual property under the agreement. Simultaneously, for a client claiming CREs under a T&M contract, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) and (e)(3) mandate that the written agreement must provide that the research is performed "on behalf of" the client, which requires that the client have a legally enforceable right to the research results, including ownership or substantial exploitation rights in the resulting formulas, processes, software, or inventions. If the contract stipulates that the performing contractor or another party holds exclusive rights to exploit the research outcomes and withholds rights from the client, the client fails the "on behalf of" / substantial rights standard and cannot claim the CRE. Moreover, as highlighted in IRS Notice 2023-63 (Example 4) comparing IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 41, if a contract places the financial risk on one party but assigns exclusive intellectual property rights to the counterparty—for instance, if a T&M contract places the financial risk on the client (because payment is hourly and non-contingent) but allows the contractor to retain exclusive ownership of the resulting IP, or if a contractor bears financial risk under a fixed-price term without retaining substantial rights—a compliance trap emerges in which neither party is eligible to claim the R&D credit: one party fails the financial risk test while the other party fails the substantial rights test. While retaining exclusive IP ownership is the safest compliance posture for the client under a T&M contract, shared, non-exclusive rights remain permissible under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(3) and Federal Circuit precedent (Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)), provided the client retains commercial exploitation rights to use the research results in its trade or business without paying additional royalties that are substantial rather than nominal.
Comparative Evaluation of Procurement Models and Risk Modifiers

The selection of a contract structure fundamentally dictates how IRS auditors allocate risk and credit eligibility between contracting counterparties. When project scope is clear and definable, commercial parties typically execute a fixed-price (lump-sum) contract, placing the risk of cost overruns and technical failure squarely on the performing contractor, who is paid only upon deliverable acceptance or milestone completion and is therefore generally eligible to claim the R&D tax credit (provided it also retains substantial rights). Conversely, when project scope is uncertain, a Straight T&M contract transfers the risk of expenditure failure to the paying client, positioning the client to claim the CRE. However, hybrid structures—such as T&M Not-to-Exceed (NTE) contracts or T&M agreements modified by warranty-of-success clauses requiring the contractor to fix errors free of charge—alter the baseline risk distribution and introduce severe audit scrutiny for both parties.

As quantified in the baseline contract risk distribution model, the interaction between payment structure, warranty guarantees, and intellectual property retention governs whether an outsourced R&D arrangement withstands IRS examination. Under the baseline risk simulator parameters, a Straight T&M contract executed on a "best efforts" basis assigns a 90 percent relative financial risk weight to the client and only a 10 percent weight to the contractor (with benefit certainty inversely distributed at 10 percent for the client and 90 percent for the contractor). Conversely, a standard Fixed-Price contract assigns a 20 percent relative financial risk weight to the client and an 80 percent weight to the contractor. Introducing a warranty-of-success clause ("Must Fix Free") that forces the contractor to remedy errors or re-execute failed designs without charge shifts 30 percentage points of financial risk away from the client and back onto the contractor, altering the Straight T&M balance from 90 percent / 10 percent to 60 percent client risk and 40 percent contractor risk—an allocation identical to the baseline of a hybrid Capped T&M (NTE) agreement. body.text: Judicial Precedent: Hybrid Contract Scrutiny and Documentation Rigor
Cost Containment Caps and Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States

Federal judicial precedent establishes strict boundaries regarding the applicability of the R&D tax credit to hybrid contract structures that incorporate cost-containment ceilings. In Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), aff'g 112 A.F.T.R.2d 2013-5488 (S.D. Fla. 2013), the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit analyzed how cost-containment mechanisms within engineering and consulting contracts affect the funded research determination under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4A(d). In that litigation, Geosyntec claimed a federal income tax refund of $1,677,432 across the 2002 through 2005 tax years. While the district court held that Geosyntec's fixed-price contracts were unfunded (resulting in a $255,575 settlement refund), the district court and the Eleventh Circuit ruled that research expenses incurred under Geosyntec's "capped contracts"—specifically the Cherry Island Landfill expansion contract with the Delaware Solid Waste Authority (capped at approximately $10 million) and the Waste Management groundwater bioremediation study contract (capped at approximately $19,000), under which Geosyntec billed monthly for labor and expenses at predefined rates up to a maximum ceiling price—fell within the funded research exclusion, rendering the performing contractor ineligible for the R&D tax credit. Applying the Federal Circuit's benchmark from Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), the Eleventh Circuit rejected Geosyntec's argument that bearing budget-overrun risk above a ceiling cap satisfied the financial risk test, holding that "cost-of-performance is not the financial risk with which we are concerned because 'the only issue is whether payment was contingent on the success of the research'—that is, the financial risk of failure." Because the clients were obligated to pay Geosyntec's monthly invoices for predefined tasks performed to professional standards regardless of whether the research achieved a successful technological outcome, the contractor did not bear the financial risk of research failure.

This judicial precedent carries critical implications for clients seeking to claim CREs under T&M Not-to-Exceed (NTE) or Cost Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF) / Cost Plus Guaranteed Maximum contracts. T&M NTE contracts are inherently hazardous for a client claiming a CRE because they introduce ambiguity regarding which party truly bears the economic risk of research failure under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii). As the Eleventh Circuit observed in Footnote 8 of Geosyntec (776 F.3d at 1341 n.8), under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e), a client may claim the research tax credit only as to those amounts that are not contingent on success. If a T&M contract stipulates that the contractor will not be reimbursed for expenses incurred above the NTE ceiling while still requiring delivery of a completed design, or requires the contractor to correct deficient work at its own expense, the financial burden of failure is partially or wholly shifted back to the contractor. The moment a T&M agreement introduces performance-based risk or a cost-containment cap that transfers financial exposure back to the performer, the client's ability to claim the CRE is jeopardized.

Specifically, if a T&M cap is set at $100,000 for a project expected to cost $50,000, the arrangement functions economically like a Straight T&M contract where the client bears the risk; conversely, if the project is likely to cost $150,000, the $100,000 cap functions like a fixed-price ceiling that shifts overrun risk onto the contractor. Consequently, hybrid T&M NTE structures create a legal gray area in which both contracting parties may be deemed ineligible for the R&D tax credit: the client fails to bear 100 percent of the non-contingent financial risk required for an unassailable CRE claim under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2), while the contractor simultaneously fails to bear sufficient success-contingent financial risk under the Geosyntec interpretation of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d). For maximum compliance clarity, Straight T&M contracts devoid of NTE caps or warranty clawbacks remain legally safer for supporting the client's CRE claim than complex hybrid instruments.
Time-Tracking Substantiation and Moore v. Commissioner

Beyond contractual risk allocation, the sufficiency of underlying documentation is decisive during an IRS examination. In Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd, No. 23-2681, 2024 WL 1881075 (7th Cir. Apr. 30, 2024), the U.S. Tax Court and the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit underscored that even when underlying R&D activities are technically legitimate, the R&D tax credit will be disallowed if the taxpayer's documentation is insufficient to distinguish qualified research time from non-qualifying activities. In Moore, the taxpayers (owners of Subchapter S scoreboard manufacturer Nevco, Inc.) allocated 65 percent of the salary and bonuses of their President and Chief Operating Officer to the R&D credit based on testimony and generalized estimates of his involvement in new product development, despite lacking written task-level time records as required under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d) (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d)). Both courts disallowed the entire wage allocation, holding that "new product development" is broader than statutory "qualified research" and that payroll records logging total hours worked without documenting the specific tasks performed cannot substantiate what fraction of time was devoted to a process of experimentation. Additionally, the Tax Court enforced the "one-up" rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2), holding that "direct supervision" of qualified research covers only immediate first-line supervision of researchers (performed at Nevco by the Director of Engineering) and excludes higher-level executive oversight ("supervision of supervision").

Because the T&M commercial model relies entirely on tracking hours worked for billing purposes, the Moore precedent and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) impose a mandatory operational requirement on the client taxpayer: the client must contractually obligate the external contractor to implement rigorous, detailed, and contemporaneous record-keeping. Furthermore, contractors must segregate direct engineering conduct and immediate first-line technical supervision from upper-level executive oversight or general project administration that would fail under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3) and § 1.41-2(e)(1). The retained documentation must be precise enough to substantiate that the claimed expenditures are eligible for the credit by providing usable, task-level detail tied to specific business components. Failure to enforce contemporaneous time-tracking standards on the contractor will lead to the disallowance of the CRE claim during an audit, regardless of how favorably the written contract allocates financial risk and intellectual property rights.
Practical Application: Contract Drafting, Substantiation, and Financial Modeling
Mandatory Contract Drafting Clauses for T&M Agreements

To ensure a client taxpayer can defensibly claim CREs under a T&M arrangement pursuant to Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2) and (e)(3), corporate legal and tax departments must incorporate three mandatory contractual elements into all Master Services Agreements (MSAs) and Statements of Work (SOWs):

items: Pre-Performance Execution (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)): Regarding timing, the contract must be executed in writing prior to the performance of the qualified research; retroactive agreements or post-performance purchase order ratifications cannot qualify prior research outlays as CREs.

Unconditional Non-Contingent Payment Risk (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)): Regarding payment risk, the agreement must explicitly state that the client is unconditionally required to bear the research expense even if the project is unsuccessful, utilizing T&M payment phrasing—such as "payable upon receipt of monthly invoice," "billed monthly for actual hours incurred," or "compensated at predetermined hourly labor rates plus direct materials on a best-efforts basis"—that guarantees compensation for time and materials regardless of technical outcome, while strictly avoiding fixed-price or success-contingent triggers like "payable upon technical acceptance," "contingent upon milestone validation," or free-rework warranty guarantees.

Research Performed "On Behalf Of" the Client and Substantial IP Rights (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) & (e)(3)): Regarding intellectual property rights, the contract must explicitly state that the research is performed on behalf of the client taxpayer and assign the client exclusive ownership or substantial, royalty-free commercial rights to exploit the resulting inventions, formulas, software, techniques, or processes.

body.text: Audit-Ready Documentation Architecture

Under IRS examination standards codified in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(d) (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d)), taxpayers claiming a credit under IRC Section 41 are required to "retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit." For T&M contracts, this compliance burden is heightened because the taxpayer's records must link every dollar of claimed QREs directly to specific research activities and business components, effectively narrating the initial technological uncertainty, the systematic experimentation undertaken, and the technical alternatives evaluated. Moreover, under the revised IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) instructions (Rev. December 2025, released February 2026), Section G (Business Component Information) becomes mandatory for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 (absent the small-filer exception for controlled groups with $1.5 million or less in QREs and $50 million or less in prior three-year average gross receipts, or a Qualified Small Business payroll tax credit election under IRC § 41(h)), requiring taxpayers to report QREs—including Contract Research Expenses—at the individual business-component level across the top 50 business components comprising at least 80 percent of total QREs.

Defensible documentation for T&M CREs therefore extends far beyond summarized monthly invoices. The client taxpayer must obtain and retain granular records from the contractor that allow the IRS to audit the specific hours claimed against the underlying experimental tasks and business components. Specifically, invoices and supporting procurement documents—including Statements of Work, purchase orders, and Master Services Agreements—must delineate the contractor's labor hours and material costs and code them directly to business components and activities that satisfy the four-part test, such as "Experimentation: Testing Prototype 3.1." The internal accounting and timekeeping systems of the external contractor must therefore be aligned with the client's R&D tax compliance protocols prior to project kickoff, ensuring the client receives auditable raw data—such as employee time-tracking logs, task descriptions, and hourly billing breakdowns—rather than high-level billing summaries. Table 2 summarizes the minimum documentation standards required for defensible T&M CRE claims.

Pre-performance execution date; clear delineation of client IP ownership or substantial rights; explicit non-contingent hourly and material payment terms; indemnification and best-efforts clauses.
Satisfies the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3) and § 1.41-4A(d) Financial Risk and Substantial Rights tests; prevents the performing contractor from claiming the credit.
Time-Tracking Data and Logs

Contemporaneous records linking individual contractor employee hours directly to qualified experimental activities (e.g., prototype testing, modeling) and specific business components, backed by timecards/registers.

Substantiates the direct nexus between labor cost and qualified research function under Moore v. Commissioner and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d); prevents inclusion of non-qualifying G&A or upper-tier oversight.
Itemized T&M Invoices

Line-item breakdown of hourly labor rates, hours worked per coded task/component, U.S. performance location, and specific tangible materials (supplies) consumed, separating overhead and administrative charges.
Verifies the exact amount paid or incurred under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1); justifies the 100% qualifying base prior to applying the 65% statutory inclusion rule.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example and Downstream Credit Modeling

In this case study, the client taxpayer, Bio-Tech Innovators, Inc. (BTI), is developing a novel chemical separation technique for a pharmaceutical process—an activity that qualifies as R&D under IRC Section 41(d)(1) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a) due to technological uncertainty regarding the appropriate separation method and design. BTI outsources the required experimental engineering work to an external contractor, Alpha Labs, under a Straight Time and Materials Contract executed in writing prior to the commencement of research.

Under the contract terms, BTI compensates Alpha Labs at a predetermined rate of $200 per hour for qualified engineering labor and reimburses Alpha Labs for all specific, required chemical supplies, billed and paid monthly. Critically, the contract stipulates that BTI must pay these billed amounts regardless of whether the chemical separation technique is successfully optimized, and BTI retains exclusive intellectual property rights to all resulting formulas. During the tax year, Alpha Labs performs all work physically within the United States and bills BTI a gross total of $135,000, consisting of 600 hours of qualified domestic engineering labor at $200 per hour ($120,000), qualified supply costs for non-depreciable chemical reagents and prototypes ($10,000), and non-qualified G&A and administrative time ($5,000) that is properly segregated on Alpha Labs' itemized invoices.

To compute its eligible Contract Research Expenses under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(1), BTI first excludes the $5,000 of non-qualified G&A and administrative charges from the $135,000 gross billing to establish the 100 percent substantiated qualified research base:
Next, BTI applies the 65 percent statutory inclusion rate under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) to the $130,000 qualified base:

The remaining 35 percent of the qualified research base ($45,500) is removed via the statutory haircut alongside the $5,000 of excluded G&A, resulting in an eligible CRE claim of $84,500. BTI successfully substantiates this $84,500 CRE claim because the Straight T&M structure demonstrates that BTI bore the unconditional financial risk of the $130,000 research expenditure proving fruitless and retained exclusive IP rights to the output, satisfying both prongs of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3) and Section 1.41-4A(d) while precluding Alpha Labs from claiming the credit for the same effort.

Once the $84,500 of eligible T&M CREs is substantiated, it serves as a foundational input for corporate tax modeling on IRS Form 6765 under the two statutory calculation methods: the Regular Research Credit (RRC, reported in Section A of Form 6765) and the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC, reported in Section B of Form 6765). Under the Regular Research Credit (RRC) method codified in IRC Section 41(a)(1) and Section 41(c)(1)–(3), the taxpayer first determines its fixed-base percentage, which for historical taxpayers is the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for tax years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (IRC § 41(c)(3)(A)), or for startup companies under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(B) starts at a statutory rate of 3 percent for each of the taxpayer's first five taxable years with QREs before transitioning over years six through ten to a historical QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio, and in all events is statutorily capped at a maximum fixed-base percentage of 16 percent under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(C). This fixed-base percentage is multiplied by the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts from the four preceding taxable years to establish the base amount under IRC Section 41(c)(1), subject to a statutory minimum base floor under IRC Section 41(c)(2) equal to 50 percent of current-year QREs (0.50 multiplied by current-year QREs). The final RRC under IRC Section 41(a)(1) is then calculated as 20 percent of the excess of current-year QREs over the applicable base amount (or 50 percent of current-year QREs, whichever base is greater):

In a modeling scenario where BTI's base amount is governed by the 50 percent statutory minimum base floor of IRC Section 41(c)(2), the $84,500 in substantiated T&M CREs increases net excess QREs by $42,250 ($84,500 multiplied by 0.50), yielding an incremental gross RRC tax benefit of $8,450 ($42,250 multiplied by 0.20) prior to any IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit adjustment.

Alternatively, corporate tax counsel should model the T&M CRE data under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method codified in IRC Section 41(c)(4)(A) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9, which provides a more direct calculation pathway for taxpayers with high historical base amounts, rapidly scaling gross receipts, or incomplete 1984–1988 historical records. The ASC method calculates the R&D credit as 14 percent of the amount by which current-year QREs exceed 50 percent of the average QREs incurred over the three preceding taxable years (or 6 percent of current-year QREs under IRC § 41(c)(4)(B) if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years):

Because the prior three-year average QRE base (50 percent of the prior three-year QRE average) is fixed at the start of the current tax year, every dollar of the $84,500 in substantiated T&M CREs above the base threshold expands the current-year excess dollar-for-dollar, generating up to $11,830 in incremental current-year gross tax credit ($84,500 multiplied by 0.14). Evaluating both calculation pathways demonstrates that rigorous T&M contract structuring and contemporaneous invoice substantiation directly drive measurable corporate tax savings, providing tax counsel with the quantitative justification necessary to enforce strict compliance standards on external contractors.
Strategic Compliance Recommendations

To maximize the financial return of Contract Research Expenses while mitigating audit exposure under IRC Section 41, corporate legal, procurement, and tax teams should integrate four strategic controls into their R&D contracting workflow:

items: Comprehensive Contractual Risk Audit: Organizations must conduct a systematic risk audit across all existing and proposed third-party research agreements, paying particular attention to hybrid instruments such as T&M Not-to-Exceed (NTE) or Cost Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF) / capped cost-plus contracts. Each contract should be evaluated against the financial risk exclusion precedent established in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(e)(2), and hybrid agreements that shift performance or overrun risk back onto the contractor via ceiling caps or free-repair warranties should be modified or replaced with Straight T&M agreements whenever the client intends to claim the CRE.

Standardized Pre-Performance Boilerplate Templates: Legal counsel should mandate standardized, research-specific contract templates for all Master Services Agreements and Statements of Work. Pursuant to 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), these templates must be executed in writing prior to research performance and explicitly incorporate unconditional, non-contingent hourly and material reimbursement terms alongside unambiguous clauses affirming that the research is performed on behalf of the client and vesting the client with exclusive or substantial royalty-free ownership of all resulting intellectual property, thereby eliminating any contractual ambiguity that could trigger the funded research exclusion or a dual-disallowance mismatch under Notice 2023-63.

Contemporaneous Task- and Component-Level Timekeeping Protocols: Procurement and tax teams must establish standardized, contemporaneous documentation protocols that contractually require external vendors to maintain time-tracking systems capable of coding labor hours directly to qualified four-part-test activities and discrete business components (satisfying both 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) and the mandatory Section G business-component reporting rules on IRS Form 6765 for tax years beginning after 2025). Rather than accepting summarized monthly invoices, the client must enforce the delivery of auditable raw time data and itemized material breakdowns generated in real time as the research is conducted, while excluding non-qualifying G&A and multi-tier executive oversight in accordance with Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd, No. 23-2681 (7th Cir. 2024).

Dual-Path RRC and ASC Financial Modeling: Tax leadership should systematically integrate substantiated T&M CRE totals into dual-path Regular Research Credit (IRC § 41(a)(1)) and Alternative Simplified Credit (IRC § 41(c)(4)) financial models—alongside IRC Section 280C(c) reduced credit elections and IRC Section 174 capitalization schedules—to quantify the exact net tax benefit generated by outsourced R&D and reinforce internal governance across engineering and procurement units.
